candidates.attacker_control: Fully attacker-controlled request body: an unauthenticated or low-privileged client can send `PATCH /{repository}/{id}` with `Content-Type: application/json-patch+json` and an array of patch operations. `JsonPatchPatchConverter.convert` takes `opNode.get("path").textValue()` and `opNode.get("from").textValue()` verbatim (JsonPatchPatchConverter.java:63-68) and constructs the operation, so every character of `path`/`from` is chosen by the caller.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that no validation exists between request body and SpEL: JsonPatchPatchConverter has no path checks; PatchOperation has no guard; JsonPatchHandler only wraps parse errors; no escaping/quoting of path nodes in PathToSpEL. Verified the parser is created with default configuration (`new SpelExpressionParser()`, PathToSpEL.java:33) and that evaluation uses plain Expression.getValue/setValue/getValueType, so no SimpleEvaluationContext or sandbox is applied. Verified the JSON converter accepts application/json-patch+json (RepositoryRestMvcConfiguration.java:481-503 lists RestMediaTypes.JSON_PATCH_JSON among supported media types) and the resolver's `converter instanceof MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter` branch is therefore taken. Checked that exceptions from evaluation are only wrapped into HttpMessageNotReadableException after the SpEL side effect (PersistentEntityResourceHandlerMethodArgumentResolver.java:202-209), and that controller-level `verifySupportedMethod`/`eTag.verify` run after argument resolution, so they do not mitigate. Searched the whole repository for other SpEL usage (`SpelExpressionParser`/`parseExpression`) and found it only in this patch package. Grepped for other high-risk sinks (Runtime.getRuntime, ObjectInputStream, XMLInputFactory, Class.forName, ScriptEngine, Jackson default typing) with no matches. The repository contains no runtime PoC or fixed variant to compare against; relation-index edges for `pathToExpression` show only test call sites because PatchOperation uses a static import, so the production call was verified directly in source text (PatchOperation.java:18, 66).
candidates.impact: Remote code execution inside the application JVM with the application's privileges: an attacker who can reach a PATCH-able repository item can cause arbitrary Java type/method invocation (process execution, file/network access, data exfiltration or tampering) while handling the request. Because the evaluation happens before any repository save or ETag verification, the side effects are not gated by application-level checks. Secondary impact includes blind information disclosure through expression evaluation.
candidates.prerequisites: (1) HTTP access to a Spring Data REST item endpoint whose repository supports PATCH (default for exported CrudRepository/PagingAndSortingRepository item resources); (2) the item id must resolve to an existing entity, because PersistentEntityResourceHandlerMethodArgumentResolver only calls readPatch when invokeFindById returns a value (lines 129-131, 175-180); (3) the deployment must not sit behind Spring Security/network rules that deny PATCH (the main source contains no authentication/authorization of its own); (4) the runtime Spring Framework must use default SpEL evaluation semantics (type references enabled), which is the default for SpelExpressionParser/StandardEvaluationContext.
candidates.root_cause: In the JSON Patch implementation, the operation `path` and `from` strings taken from the request body are split on '/' and re-assembled into a SpEL expression string with no validation or escaping (PathToSpEL.pathNodesToSpEL appends each non-numeric path node verbatim). The expression is parsed by a plain `new SpelExpressionParser()` and later evaluated through `Expression.getValue(target)` / `setValue(target, value)` / `getValueType(target)`, i.e. against a default StandardEvaluationContext with unrestricted type/method resolution. Because the '/' split is the only transformation, SpEL metacharacters in a path node (type references, method calls, property traversal) survive and are interpreted as an expression rather than as a literal property path.
candidates.title: Attacker-controlled JSON Patch path/from values are parsed and evaluated as SpEL, leading to remote code execution
candidates.trace: 1) `RepositoryEntityController.patchItemResource` (lines 385-399) maps PATCH /{repository}/{id} and declares a `PersistentEntityResource` argument. 2) Spring MVC resolves that argument with `PersistentEntityResourceHandlerMethodArgumentResolver.resolveArgument` (lines 110-157); it looks up the existing entity by id and, for a PATCH request read by a Jackson converter, calls `readPatch` (lines 172-180). 3) `readPatch` (lines 195-210) builds `new JsonPatchHandler(mapper, reader)` and calls `handler.apply(request, existingObject)`. 4) `JsonPatchHandler.apply`/`applyPatch` (lines 76-92) parse the body with `new JsonPatchPatchConverter(mapper).convert(...)` (lines 109-117). 5) `JsonPatchPatchConverter.convert` (lines 50-88) extracts `op`, `path`, `value`, `from` from the untrusted JSON array and constructs ReplaceOperation/TestOperation/RemoveOperation/AddOperation/CopyOperation/MoveOperation instances. 6) Each operation's constructor reaches `PatchOperation(String op, String path, Object value)` (lines 61-67) which calls `pathToExpression(path)` (static import at line 18). 7) `PathToSpEL.pathToExpression` (lines 42-44) turns the path into a SpEL string via `pathNodesToSpEL` (lines 70-113), which appends non-numeric nodes verbatim (line 102), and parses it with the shared `SpelExpressionParser` (line 33). 8) `Patch.apply` then invokes `operation.perform`; `TestOperation.perform` calls `getValueFromTarget` -> `spelExpression.getValue(target)` (PatchOperation.java:174-181), `ReplaceOperation.perform` calls `setValueOnTarget` -> `spelExpression.setValue(target, value)` (PatchOperation.java:164-166), and late-value evaluation calls `spelExpression.getValueType(target)` (PatchOperation.java:192-196). These calls evaluate the attacker-controlled expression; any SpEL side effects (Java type/method resolution) occur before the resulting value is used, and all of this happens during argument resolution, i.e. before the controller's `verifySupportedMethod`/ETag handling. 9) The `from` field of copy/move operations takes the same path into `pathToExpression` (CopyOperation.java:58-61; JsonPatchPatchConverter.java:68,78-81).
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: no code was compiled or executed and no request was sent. The exact SpEL capabilities depend on the Spring Framework version pulled from the external spring-data-parent/Spring BOM (this snapshot only pins BUILD-SNAPSHOT parents), although the code path uses default SpelExpressionParser/StandardEvaluationContext semantics. Whether an individual deployment restricts PATCH via Spring Security or network policy is application-specific, and the requirement that the target entity already exists at the requested id is a precondition confirmed in source.
candidates.weakness_type: Expression language (SpEL) injection leading to remote code execution (CWE-917 / CWE-94)

coverage_summary: Scope: 452 files under the assigned root (451 model-visible; 1 excluded by the run's sensitive-name/path filter; binaries skipped by NUL-byte policy). The P1 relation index parsed 410 Java files into 4,073 symbols / 6,392 edges / 11,142 calls with 0 parse errors, but it is syntax-only: no control-flow, data-flow, or semantic resolution, 8,863 unresolved calls, and 35 files (mostly non-Java resources) omitted from the index, so index absence is not evidence of absence. Reviewed in source: the full JSON Patch package (PathToSpEL, PatchOperation and all operation subclasses, JsonPatchPatchConverter, JsonPatchHandler), the argument resolver that feeds it (PersistentEntityResourceHandlerMethodArgumentResolver), the PATCH route and repository controllers, RepositoryRestMvcConfiguration converter/resolver registration, RepositoryRestHandlerMapping/CORS accessor, BaseUri, DomainObjectReader, and the relevant patch/CORS tests plus relation-index facts for routes/tests. Test modules (JPA/MongoDB/Gemfire/Solr/security) were used as navigation hints and spot-checked rather than reviewed line-by-line. No compilation, execution, or runtime testing was performed.
limitations: Static source review only; no runtime confirmation, compilation, test execution, or exploit payloads.
Dependency versions are not resolvable from the snapshot (parent POMs are BUILD-SNAPSHOT), so the exact Spring Framework SpEL semantics and default evaluation context could not be verified locally.

P1 relation index is partial and syntax-based: no data/control flow, 8,863 unresolved calls, 35 files omitted from the index; static-import call sites (e.g. PatchOperation -> PathToSpEL.pathToExpression) are not represented and were verified manually.
One file was excluded by the run's safety filter and could not be inspected.
Non-Java resources, distribution/hal-browser modules, and most test modules were not exhaustively read; findings about them are limited to targeted searches.
Whether a deployment blocks the PATCH endpoint via Spring Security or network policy is environment-specific and unverified.

rejected_leads.lead: Permissive CORS defaults for @CrossOrigin-annotated repositories (allowed origins/headers default to '*', allowCredentials true) in RepositoryRestHandlerMapping.RepositoryCorsConfigurationAccessor (lines 289-329)
rejected_leads.reason: The permissive values are inherited from Spring's own @CrossOrigin defaults and only take effect when a repository interface is explicitly annotated with @CrossOrigin; the test RepositoryCorsConfigurationAccessorUnitTests (lines 64-72) codifies this as intended behavior. It is a configuration-hardening concern, not attacker-controlled input executing a dangerous sink, and is much weaker evidence than the SpEL injection.

rejected_leads.lead: RepositoryRestHandlerMapping/BaseUri lookup-path handling (e.g. lookupPath.replaceAll("//", "/") in BaseUri.java:115 and base-URI stripping) possibly enabling path confusion
rejected_leads.reason: No concrete traversal/authorization bypass could be traced in this revision; the normalization only affects handler/CORS mapping decisions and repository resources are still matched against configured export mappings. Not enough source evidence for a vulnerability claim.

rejected_leads.lead: DomainObjectReader merge/PUT handling (DomainObjectReader.java:81-180) potentially mass-assigning identifiers/associations from request JSON
rejected_leads.reason: The reader explicitly walks the persistent-entity model with association handlers and mapped-property tracking; no bypass of id/association protections was demonstrated from source, and the JSON/merge-PATCH path does not use SpEL. Kept as an unconfirmed hardening lead only.

This route uses @RequestBody Resources<Object> and the URI-list/JSON link model, not the JSON Patch converter, so it is not on the SpEL injection path; singular-property PATCH is explicitly rejected (lines 310-315). No independent vulnerability evidence found.
No enableDefaultTyping/activating polymorphic typing was found in the source snapshot, and no other dangerous deserialization sink was identified.

summary: Spring Data REST 3.0.0.BUILD-SNAPSHOT (spring-data-rest-webmvc). The JSON Patch pipeline builds SpEL expressions directly from attacker-supplied patch `path` (and `from`) values and evaluates them with a default StandardEvaluationContext while resolving a PATCH request argument. A PATCH request to any exported repository item endpoint with Content-Type application/json-patch+json lets a caller inject SpEL into the patch path; evaluation happens during argument resolution (before controller-level method/ETag checks) and can invoke Java types/methods, i.e., remote code execution in the application JVM. This is the strongest candidate found; weaker leads are listed as rejected.
